blocks.text: Keeping Autocomplete Fresh and Safe: The Pipeline Behind the Dropdown

The second half of the autocomplete design: the log pipeline that learns what the world is asking, the freshness overlay that hears breaking news in minutes, and the policy gate that exists because of one bad December night in 2016.
9:02 a.m.: the dropdown meets a world it has never seen

Picture a Tuesday morning. At 9:02, something happens — an earthquake, a cup final draw, a rocket launch, pick your headline — and within ninety seconds, a million people are typing its name into a search box. Every one of them gets suggestions from a snapshot built last night, from searches counted up to yesterday. The new query isn't in the trie. It isn't in any top-10 list. As far as the dropdown is concerned, the most important question in the world this morning does not exist.

The previous lesson built the serving half of autocomplete: a trie with precomputed answers, sharded, cached, answering in tens of milliseconds. It ended with a promise — the snapshot is built, by a pipeline. This lesson builds the pipeline, and it has three jobs, in ascending order of how badly things go when they're skipped:
Learn what the world asks (count the query log, with decay).
Stay current (hear this morning's spike in minutes, not at tomorrow's rebuild).
Stay decent (never let the counts repeat the ugliest thing in the room back to a billion people).
Job 3 has a date attached to it: December 2016. We'll get there — it's the reason this lesson exists as its own lesson.
Picture the friend again — the habits that keep them current
Recall the friend who finishes your sentences. Last lesson mechanized two of their habits: they've heard everything, and they keep shortlists ready. Two more habits run this lesson:

They update with the times. Last year "how do I get tickets to—" ended with a concert; this week it ends with the final. Their shortlist decays the old and promotes the suddenly-asked. Mechanized: counting with decay, plus a live overlay for what's spiking now.

They have tact. Some endings they could say, they don't — the rude, the hateful, the harmful. A pure popularity machine has no tact. Mechanized: screening and a policy gate that sit between the counts and the user, permanently.
The counting pipeline: from keystrokes to snapshot
Walk it once, slowly:

Log everything. Every executed search — the final query the user actually ran, not every keystroke — is appended to a query log stream. (Keystrokes are noise; submitted queries are intent. The message-queues lesson is this stream's home turf.)

Stream branch: windowed counting → the freshness overlay. As searches stream in, windowed counters tally them over the last minutes and hours. Counting billions of distinct queries exactly, live, is a memory bonfire, so this branch counts approximately, using the counting-sketch family (count-min is the famous one): keep a small fixed table of counters, hash each query into a few slots and bump those counters, and estimate a query's count as the smallest of its slots — collisions with other queries can only push an estimate up, never down. A tail query's count being off by a little changes nothing that matters; exactness is spent on the head, the tail gets statistics. This branch's output is the freshness overlay: the last few hours of fast-rising queries.

Batch branch: daily counts, decay, screening → the trie builder. On a slower cadence, a batch job aggregates the log into per-query counts. Raw all-time counts would embalm the past — a query everyone asked in 2019 would outrank what the world asked this morning — so counts decay: recent days weigh more than old ones. Frequency is a memory with a half-life: with a 7-day half-life (an illustrative choice, not a law), a search from 7 days ago counts half as much as the same search today, and a quarter as much after 14 days. Before the build, the aggregated counts pass a policy screening stage — denylists and classifiers for the categories the policy filter bans (hateful, sexually explicit, dangerous). Screening at build time is cheaper than apologizing at press time; this lesson's war story is the receipt.

Build and version the trie. The builder emits a complete new snapshot — compressed trie, top-k lists, ID table — stamped with a version. Serving nodes load it beside the old one and swap atomically; a half-loaded index is never served. Versioning sounds like bookkeeping until the first bad build; then it's the difference between "roll back to v41" and an incident.

The freshness overlay — the stream branch's output — is a small, separate, in-memory structure holding the last few hours of fast-rising queries. The score it uses is a ratio, not a count — this hour's rate versus this query's own baseline — so a query jumping from 10 searches a day to 10,000 an hour outranks queries with a million sleepy all-time searches. At read time the serving tier merges the snapshot's top-k with the overlay's spiking completions for that prefix. Batch gives you the truth; the overlay gives you this morning. Google's own description of its predictions lists "trending interest in a query" as a ranking factor — this overlay is how a design earns that line.

The merge is the reconciliation point between two honest sources of truth, and it has rules: the snapshot's list is the base (stable, screened, complete); overlay entries are admitted only if they pass the same policy screening (spikes are exactly where manipulation lives — see below); and each overlay entry expires in hours, so yesterday's spike can't squat in the list after the world moves on.
The night the dropdown embarrassed Google

December 2016. A Guardian journalist, Carole Cadwalladr, is writing about how search shapes what people believe. She types seven letters — are jews — and the dropdown offers to finish: are jews evil? She tries are women: the dropdown offers are women evil? The suggestions weren't written by anyone at Google. They were real searches, counted faithfully — enough people had asked those questions that a pure popularity ranking floated them to the top, no human judgment anywhere in the loop. Google removed the specific suggestions within days and confirmed the removal to the Guardian and the Telegraph. A spokesperson's defence was honest and damning at once: autocomplete "isn't an exact science," and about 15 percent of each day's searches are entirely new — the corpus is a live feed of humanity, unfiltered.

Hold this story next to the pipeline diagram and the design writes itself: every stage that touches the ranking is a place where judgment either exists or doesn't. Counts without screening made the dropdown a mirror that repeated the ugliest thing in the room at the volume it was shouted. So the production design layers its defences:
Build-time screening (the batch branch, above): denylists + classifiers over the aggregated corpus, before anything reaches a snapshot.

Overlay screening: the freshness path is the manipulable path — a brigade can manufacture a "spike" — so overlay promotions pass the same screen, plus a higher evidence bar (sustained rate from diverse sources, not a burst from a botnet-shaped one).

A kill switch: a human-review channel that can pull a live suggestion in minutes without a rebuild — because the next embarrassing suggestion is, by definition, the one the classifiers didn't know about.
The gate at read time (previous lesson): policy flags travel with the snapshot, and the serving tier drops flagged completions regardless of score.
"How do you keep the suggestions from embarrassing you?" is a top-three follow-up in this interview. Have the story ready; have the layers designed.
Unhappy paths, and how the design reconciles them
The previous lesson's walkthrough was the happy path. Here is everything else, and the layer that absorbs each blow:

A story breaks and the snapshot is stale. The 9:02 a.m. problem from the opener. Reconciliation: the freshness overlay — stream-counted spikes merge at read time, so the dropdown learns in minutes while the snapshot stays the stable base. Two sources of truth, reconciled per-request, each with its own TTL.

A suggestion goes viral for the wrong reason. A coordinated campaign pumps a hateful query's count until raw frequency would rank it first — December 2016 as a load pattern. Reconciliation: the policy layers above. Frequency proposes; policy disposes — at build time, in the overlay, and at the gate.

The counts themselves are gamed. Bots submit searches to manufacture a trend. Reconciliation: the pipeline counts distinct, human-looking demand — it can weight by user diversity and drop traffic that fails the same bot checks the search front door uses. A trend that only exists inside one datacenter's worth of fake users isn't a trend.

A bad build ships. A buggy aggregation job emits a snapshot with corrupted top-k lists. Reconciliation: snapshots are versioned and swapped atomically; the previous version stays loaded beside the new one, so rollback is a pointer flip — and canary shards (a small subset of shards that receive the new snapshot first and are watched for errors while the rest of the fleet stays on the old version) serve it to a slice of traffic before the fleet commits; only if they stay healthy does the rollout continue.

The prefix matches nothing. Fast typists and new words constantly produce prefixes with no completions — Mitra and Craswell (2015) call these rare prefixes. Reconciliation: degrade gracefully — back off to the longest prefix that does have a list, or run a spelling-tolerant match; if still nothing, return empty. The friend who finishes your sentences is allowed to say "no idea." Inventing completions is the one unforgivable sin.

See the pattern: the read path is never allowed to improvise, and the write path is never allowed to be naive. Every surprise is absorbed by a layer designed for it — overlay for freshness, screening for safety, versions for bad builds, diversity checks for gamers.
Interview follow-ups (they will ask)

"Add personalization." Merge a per-user list — built from the user's own search history by the same log pipeline at user scope — ahead of the global top-10, clearly budgeted (say 2–3 slots) so personal history sharpens rather than hijacks the list. Google's help page confirms personal history is one of its real factors.

"Your user can't spell." Typo tolerance: match against the trie with a small edit-distance budget, or keep a parallel structure of common misspellings harvested from the log (people who typed desing then immediately searched design taught you the mapping for free). Bloomberg's reported 60–80 ms figure already includes spelling correction.

"Why did Google kill Instant, then?" Because Instant's other half — repainting results per keystroke — was removed in July 2017 because of mobile; the suggestions survived. Knowing which half died, and why, is the difference between trivia and judgment.

"What breaks first at 10× scale?" Not the trie — memory shards linearly. The aggregation pipeline and the freshness overlay feel it first: counting and merging are the write-heavy parts, and write-heavy parts are where scale goes to collect its debts. (The stream-processing lessons later in the course pick this up.)
The full architecture, both halves

Read it as a loop, not a stack: the world's searches flow down into logs; the pipeline distills them into snapshots and spikes; the serving tier merges the two at read time; the answers shape what the world searches next. The dropdown is a mirror the system holds up to its own users — this lesson was about who polishes the mirror, how often, and what they're allowed to refuse to reflect.
Takeaways
Suggestions are learned, not authored: a log pipeline counts real searches with decay, approximates the tail, screens against policy, and ships versioned snapshots that serving nodes swap atomically.

Freshness is a separate layer, not a faster rebuild: a stream-fed overlay scores queries by rate versus their own baseline and merges at read time, so breaking stories appear in minutes while the batch snapshot stays the stable base.

Ranking = decayed frequency + trending boost, gated by policy at every layer — build-time screening, overlay screening, a human kill switch, and the read-time gate. December 2016 is the permanent proof that a popularity machine without those layers becomes a headline.

Every failure has a designed absorber: stale snapshot → overlay; gamed counts → diversity weighting; bad build → versioned rollback and canaries; no match → graceful backoff to a shorter prefix or an honest empty list.
